t:
(a) None of the funds provided by this or previous appropriations Acts may be obligated for deployment or implementation, on other than a test basis, of the Secure Flight program or any other follow-on or successor passenger prescreening program, until the Secretary of Homeland Security certifies, and the Government Accountability Office reports, to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, that all ten of the conditions contained in paragraphs (1) through (10) of section 522(a) of Public Law 108–334 (118 Stat. 1319) have been successfully met. 
    (b) The report required by subsection (a) shall be submitted within 90 days after the Secretary provides the requisite certification, and periodically thereafter, if necessary, until the Government Accountability Office confirms that all ten conditions have been successfully met. 
    (c) Within 90 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall submit to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives a detailed plan that describes: (1) the dates for achieving key milestones, including the date or timeframes that the Secretary will certify the program under subsection (a); and (2) the methodology to be followed to support the Secretary’s certification, as required under subsection (a). 
    (d) During the testing phase permitted by subsection (a), no information gathered from passengers, foreign or domestic air carriers, or reservation systems may be used to screen aviation passengers, or delay or deny boarding to such passengers, except in instances where passenger names are matched to a Government watch list. 
    (e) None of the funds provided in this or previous appropriations Acts may be utilized to develop or test algorithms assigning risk to passengers whose names are not on Government watch lists. 
    (f) None of the funds provided in this or any other Act may be used for data or a database that is obtained from or remains under the control of a non-Federal entity: Provided, That this 
restriction shall not apply to Passenger Name Record data obtained from air carriers.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the certification, GAO report, and detailed plan are procedural checks on a federal decision, and that the mentions of passengers, air carriers, and non-Federal entities bring in outside parties. But the certification and reporting run only between the Secretary, GAO, and congressional committees, all of which are inside the federal government. Passengers, air carriers, and non-Federal entities appear only as sources of data, not as parties consulted on or able to challenge a federal decision. The section provides no comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation, or right to sue.
fable.s: until the Secretary of Homeland Security certifies, and the Government Accountability Office reports, to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives

qwen_block.w: This section restricts the use of funds until specific certifications and reports are submitted to Congressional committees. Congress and its committees are inside the federal government, so reporting to them is not participation by outside parties. The Government Accountability Office is also a federal agency. There is no requirement for consultation with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities before the decision to deploy the program.
qwen_block.s: None of the funds provided by this or previous appropriations Acts may be obligated for deployment or implementation, on other than a test basis, of the Secure Flight program or any other follow-on or successor passenger prescreening program, until the Secretary of Homeland Security certifies, and the Government Accountability Office reports, to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, that all ten of the conditions contained in paragraphs (1) through (10) of section 522(a) of Public Law 108–334 (118 Stat. 1319) have been successfully met.

opus.w: The only process before deployment is a certification by the DHS Secretary and a report by GAO to congressional Appropriations Committees. All of these actors are inside the federal government. Passengers, air carriers and non-Federal entities appear only as sources of data subject to funding limits. They are not consulted, given a hearing or comment period, or granted a right to challenge the decision, so the outside-party requirement is not met.
opus.s: until the Secretary of Homeland Security certifies, and the Government Accountability Office reports, to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, that all ten of the conditions contained in paragraphs (1) through (10) of section 522(a) of Public Law 108–334 (118 Stat. 1319) have been successfully met.
opus.b:
I'd label this **No**. The tempting reading is that the section mentions outside parties (passengers, air carriers, reservation systems and non-Federal entities) and sets up a formal certification and reporting process before a federal decision. But that doesn't meet the definition:

- **The decision process stays inside the federal government.** Before Secure Flight can be deployed, the Secretary of Homeland Security must certify, GAO must report, and the plan goes to the Appropriations Committees. Every one of these actors is federal.
- **The outsiders only appear as sources of data.** Passengers and air carriers supply information that is subject to funding limits. Nobody outside the government is consulted, given a hearing or comment period, or given a right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires certifications and reports to be submitted to Congressional committees and the Government Accountability Office. Both Congress and the GAO are part of the federal government (inside the boundary). There is no requirement to consult, coordinate with, or seek input from any outside parties (such as the public, states, or private companies) before making the decision to deploy the program. The restriction on using data from non-Federal entities is a limitation on data sources, not a participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: None of the funds provided by this or previous appropriations Acts may be obligated for deployment or implementation, on other than a test basis, of the Secure Flight program or any other follow-on or successor passenger prescreening program, until the Secretary of Homeland Security certifies, and the Government Accountability Office reports, to the Committees on Appropriations of the Senate and the House of Representatives, that all ten of the conditions contained in paragraphs (1) through (10) of section 522(a) of Public Law 108–334 (118 Stat. 1319) have been successfully met.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Secretary to submit a plan or report to Congress constitutes "participation" because it involves external oversight. However, Congress is explicitly defined as being INSIDE the federal government. Therefore, reporting to Congress is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties. The section also restricts the use of data from non-Federal entities (air carriers), but this is a prohibition on data usage, not a requirement for consultation, coordination, or advisory input from those entities before a decision is made. The GAO report is also an internal government audit function.
